approach.method_basis: The Parent evolves a live population of scored molecular graphs. It keeps the highest-scoring survivors, favors their upper score bands when choosing parents, and makes new graphs through mutation chains and connected-fragment crossover. Every accepted score also enters a complete archive used by a count-fingerprint Gaussian process to choose each evaluation batch from a larger candidate pool. Direct aromatic carbon/nitrogen exchange is disabled. Accepted offspring can become parents, while the best observed molecule remains in the population.
approach.novelty: This control tests the contribution of greedy survival among records other than the incumbent. It always keeps the inherited best record, fills the remaining survivor places with the most recently accepted records still in the live contest, and restores the original score order before breeding. Unlike the initial-cohort and uniform-parent controls, it keeps recursive breeding and the original rank preference. Unlike the recent-batch tie experiment, it deliberately removes competition by strict score among nonincumbents. Retention receipts will be followed through actual breeding support, draws and evaluated descendants; recency is an explicit contribution control, not a proposed performance gain.

hypothesis: Replace only nonincumbent score-greedy survivor membership with the newest accepted serials from the current live retention contest, protecting the single inherited incumbent and restoring inherited score/serial order before unchanged breeding.

finding_summary.headline: Nonincumbent greedy survival contributes: recency changes breeding and lowers mean final score by 0.011807.
finding_summary.insights:
The result supplies positive conditional evidence for inherited nonincumbent greedy survival while the incumbent, score-quantile sampling, recursive feedback and learned allocation stay active. Its observed route is changed access to shared survivors, rather than reuse of the extra weak records kept at the local cutoff. The latter route is explicitly refuted here. Most changed memberships leave the immediate sampling probabilities unchanged; preserving a molecule is therefore not the same as exploring its neighborhood. Earlier protected-but-never-bred retention failures remain relevant counterexamples.

The shared-survivor route can still produce useful chemistry: a crossover involving a parent newly inside sampling support creates a halogen-free aromatic/carbonyl leader and then breeds 243 times. Another such crossover loses to its parents and never breeds again. The molecular assessment finds many tiny recency-only records and 16 tiny final survivors, alongside useful amines and carbonyl frameworks and persistent reactive bonds, unusual rings and unspecified stereochemistry. These observations explain what was retained and used; they do not establish a chemical cause of the aggregate loss, graph-equivalence guarantees, or practical chemical feasibility.

This answers the specified retention-component contrast on the complete three-seed panel. It leaves membership quality, age, rank changes and later learning bundled together, and does not measure the whole evolutionary foundation or combine additively with the separate rank-preference and recursive-breeding controls. The six endpoint gains and the zero-use pathways limit transfer beyond the registered conditions. No age-window or retention retuning is justified by this completed control.
finding_summary.results:
The rule executed exactly in all 4,365 retention calls. It changed 3,483 of 3,540 capacity-limited survivor sets and 3,451 retained score vectors while preserving the incumbent. Stored alternatives did not become new breeders: none of the 135 recency-only records ever gained later sampling support or bred. Shared survivors did change ranks and probabilities, producing 3,865 altered-rank parent draws and 713 altered-probability draws. Their accepted products numbered 126 and 18 respectively, with the latter inside the former; three of the 126 raised the incumbent and 58 later bred. Two task/seed sessions had affected draws but no immediately accepted product in this locally tagged cohort.

All three replicas completed. Mean final Top -1 fell from 0.595670 to 0.583863, a paired change of -0.011807 beyond the registered 0.002 scale. Seed changes were -0.044786, +0.024951 and -0.015585. Nine task/seed endpoints declined and six improved; decoration hopping, docking and median-task means declined, while zaleplon and sitagliptin means improved. Seed-macro population deviation fell from 0.026593 to 0.002305. All 4,350 accepted products survived their immediate batch and 2,746 later bred, versus 3,415 and 2,401 under the Parent, yet this greater survival and reuse did not produce a higher endpoint mean.

molecular.headline: Aromatic carbonyl and amine families persist; recency-only survivors stay outside breeding support.
molecular.overall_character:
The complete Child and matched Parent panels cover all five objectives and Search seeds 0, 1 and 2: 4,500 scored records per node, including 4,350 accepted optimizer products and 150 initial records. All 30 trusted trajectories and 30 corresponding candidate logs were read. Each task has 870 optimizer products across its three seeds. All fifteen Child/Parent trajectories differ, with no score disagreement for a shared molecular identity within a matched task/seed. There are no missing paths or unmatched seeds. Source, trajectory, log and historical-evidence hashes, molecule descriptors, chronological provenance and trusted citations are retained in .slots/r0020-02-ablation-L01/molecular/; trajectory_chemistry_audit.json, retention_exposure_audit.json, selected_chemistry_audit.json and validation.json are the detailed receipts.

These are mostly aromatic, heteroatom-rich ring assemblies with amides, ketones, cyclic carbonyls, imines, ethers and amines, often heavily modified by halogens. Median heavy-atom counts in the fixed task order are 25, 31, 31, 31 and 27, versus Parent 25, 33, 31, 30 and 27. Overall the Child median is 29 heavy atoms and four perceived rings; individual evaluated structures range from one to 107 heavy atoms. Within each seed, related aromatic/carbonyl or aryl-amine families recur despite many distinct strings. Across all optimizer rows, Child / Parent molecule counts are 897 / 1,042 with N–halogen bonds, 456 / 278 with O–halogen bonds, 319 / 273 with O–O bonds, 24 / 17 with ring triple bonds, and 25 / 42 with a ring carbon carrying two double bonds. These flags overlap and are structural cautions, not measured stability, synthesis, toxicity or safety outcomes. Useful halogen-free leaders and conventional amine/carbonyl arrangements are counterexamples to a universal requirement for reactive bonds. RDKit identifies unassigned stereocentres in 2,553 / 2,408 molecules; no stereochemical assignments appear in the Child digest counters.

Retention and real chemical use differ sharply. Of 135 distinct records retained against a same-contest greedy cap, 125 are generated accepted products and ten are initial records. Their median size is three heavy atoms, with 79 at most three heavy atoms; larger examples include modified heterocyclic carbonyls and duplicated multiring frameworks. Although 124 subsequently occur in a live breeding population, none reaches positive breeding support or is drawn after its first recency-only retention. Eleven never appear in a later live state, including two first protected during terminal feedback. This is a measured lack of downstream use of that particular set, not absence of other chemically useful recency-retained records. The comparison is always the current Child live population plus the newly accepted record, never a resurrected archive or a separately executed greedy future.

The other observed route involves shared survivors whose ranks change. Their actual draws enter 3,051 pool products and 126 evaluated products: 12 exceed the best generating-parent score, four tie and 110 fall below it; three update the sequential incumbent, 58 later breed and 51 remain in final populations. The subset with changed sampling probability enters 548 pool products and 18 evaluations, with three parent beats and one incumbent update; these cohorts overlap. One session leader comes from a shared parent promoted across the support boundary, described below. Unqueried pool products have no assigned outcomes. Across all products, every Child product survives its immediate batch, versus 3,415 for the Parent; 2,746 / 2,401 distinct products later breed and 960 / 960 remain at termination. The Child final survivors include 16 tiny fragments versus none for the Parent, as well as 238 N–halogen-, 134 O–halogen- and 63 O–O-bearing records versus 287, 55 and 38. Final membership is not validation of chemistry. The last 150 evaluated products per node have no later breeding opportunity; the terminal leaders in two sessions cannot support a descendant claim.

The supplied complete paired mean is 0.583862951276973 versus 0.5956696497334577, with seed changes -0.04478568415133899, +0.02495097723246098 and -0.015585388450575999. Six task/seed endpoints improve and nine decline. These outcomes accompany changed chemistry; they do not identify a molecular mediator. The scoped control leaves incumbent protection, score-quantile sampling and partner exclusion, recursive accepted-offspring breeding, the complete accepted archive and active count-GP allocation in place. Historical recent-tie retention n-03acfe1ba8af also had 145 newly protected records that never subsequently bred, despite other rank-based exposure; older core-round retention n-28dc36ed5be7 had 602 directly protected records outside later support under a different Parent and profile. Their losses and limitations remain counterexamples. Uniform-live breeding n-a56491c332aa and initial-cohort breeding n-4d4b5eafa8b3 address different conditional boundaries on the shared current Parent, not independent or additive whole-foundation effects. The supplied catalog still has incomplete historical review and partial L07 ordinary-continuation composition. This assessment neither closes those gaps nor decides activation, contribution or eligibility.

per_task.generated_character:
The 870 products are mainly medium-sized indole-like, ring-expanded nitrogen heterocycle and aryl-carbonyl structures: median 25 heavy atoms and three perceived rings, with 375 N–halogen-bearing molecules. Seed 0 evaluation 207 reaches 0.459794 with a 24-heavy-atom, four-ring methoxy/methyl-substituted assembly bearing an N-amino aryl amide and a thiol substituent. It is halogen-free. Seed 1 evaluation 269 reaches 0.440491 with a 25-heavy-atom aromatic nitrogen ring expanded to nine atoms, an N–Br bond and a pyridyl ester. Seed 2 evaluation 187 reaches 0.433013 with a 24-heavy-atom indole/pyridyl ketone carrying N-vinyl and O-vinyl substituents, without halogens. These are distinct chemical organizations, not uniform enrichment of one halogenated motif.

The Parent leaders instead include a cumulated-carbon anilino/pyridyl arrangement in seed 0, an N-fluorinated heteroaryl amide in seed 1, and an N-chlorinated aryl dicarbonyl in seed 2. Complete matched final-best Child / Parent scores are seed 0: 0.459794 / 0.394051 (+0.065743); seed 1: 0.440491 / 0.474117 (-0.033626); seed 2: 0.433013 / 0.438973 (-0.005960).

The seed 2 leader is a recorded pure-crossover product. One shared survivor, the brominated indole/unsaturated seven-membered oxygen-ring ketone at evaluation 154 (0.339176), occupies actual partner rank 31 versus rank 32 under the last same-contest greedy list; the other parent scores 0.423990. The product exceeds that better parent by 0.009022 and later serves in 243 breeding draws, yet its final session endpoint remains below the matched Parent. This links real chemistry to a used shared survivor, not a directly recency-only molecule or proof that a particular inherited group caused success. Across this task, 51 evaluated products have a shared changed-rank parent: five parent beats, three ties and 43 losses. The 25 directly recency-only records never breed after protection.
liabilities: Frequent N–halogen substitution, an N-amino amide, a charged N–N environment and a nine-member aromatic nitrogen ring warrant compound-specific feasibility assessment. Parsing and high scores are insufficient evidence of makeability.

Twenty-five products have at most three heavy atoms, and recency can retain such fragments without giving them later reproductive access; membership is not evidence that useful chemical coverage increased.
missing_features: The evaluated panel does not show a consistently ordinary-bond, chemically coherent series preserving its better aromatic/carbonyl arrangements across ring-size changes; the halogen-free leaders show that a blanket halogen requirement would be wrong.

Controlled stereochemical and geometric alternatives are not demonstrated. Scalar scores do not reveal which unobserved target motif, if any, is missing; absence from the evaluated stream cannot establish absence from unscored proposals.
per_task.score_gradient_reading:
The observed gradient favors a substantial aromatic carbonyl framework over stripped fragments. Initial seed 0 evaluation 9, a trimethoxy indole carboxamide, scores 0.305105; the highest 50 products have median 25 heavy atoms, while the lowest 50 have median 3.5. Vinyl fluoride at seed 0 evaluation 257 scores zero. Size alone does not account for the gradient: ring rearrangements, carbonyl placement and substitution change the scores within similarly sized families.

Higher scores coexist with questionable bonds. Seed 0 evaluation 222 reaches 0.449897 with both N–Cl and N–F, while the halogen-free seed 0 leader scores higher. The charged N–N carbonyl substituent at evaluation 213 reaches 0.425403, beats its generating parent and later breeds 105 times. Thus neither N–halogen presence nor absence is a general score explanation. The final seed 0 product at evaluation 300 falls to 0.377678 while carrying an N–S–Cl branch and N–F; retained incumbent score should not be confused with that last product.

None of 25 directly recency-only records later breeds. This includes seed 1 evaluation 59, the three-heavy-atom O–F fragment at score 0.5, which remains in six subsequent live states without support, and seed 0 evaluation 229, an N-chlorinated fused dicarbonyl at 0.545618, which reaches two later live states without support. liabilities: There are 181 O–halogen-, 240 O–O- and 24 ring-triple-bond-bearing products, versus Parent 89, 218 and 17. These overlapping groups include peroxide/hypohalite environments and constrained ring unsaturation that require local chemical assessment.

Crowded fused systems, unusual carbon substitution and occasional very large assemblies coexist with the aromatic frameworks. Recency-only preservation gives no synthesis or stability evidence, and the directly protected examples supply no descendant outcomes.
missing_features: A consistently feasible set of alternative linker and ring connections preserving the higher-scoring heteroaryl/carbonyl organization is not established. Scalar ties tolerate materially different reactive substitutions.

The evaluated higher-ring-count products do not demonstrate reliable improvement through controlled scaffold reorganization; unscored pool structures cannot be assigned the same limitation without labels.
per_task.score_gradient_reading:
The initial seed 0 aromatic cyclic-dione/ester at evaluation 7 scores 0.548381. Larger, connected heteroaryl carbonyl organizations rise above the 0.5 fragment floor; the highest 50 Child products have median 30 heavy atoms and four aromatic rings, versus 7.5 heavy atoms in the lowest 50. The observed association does not imply that maximizing ring number is useful: the seven-ring seed 0 leader remains far below its matched Parent.

Different chemistry can share the same top score: seed 1 evaluation 224 has methoxy and O–Br substituents, while evaluation 234 replaces the methoxy organization with another O–Br-containing arrangement and still scores 0.643167. Forty-six of the highest 50 products carry O–halogen bonds. This is evidence of tolerance in the recorded score, not a demonstrated need for those bonds or a chemically validated analogue series.

Seed 1 evaluation 275 reaches 0.999994 with a 30-heavy-atom aryl ether/ring assembly, a tertiary chain amine, an aminomethyl branch and a thiol. Seed 2 evaluation 271 reaches 0.993355 with a 31-heavy-atom N-propyl piperidine/biaryl arrangement containing a fused four-member carbocycle, amino/fluoromethyl substitution and an O–S branch.

The Parent leaders likewise combine substituted aromatic groups with chain or ring amines, including a dibromophenyl dialkylamine in seed 0 and fused aryl/ring-amine systems in seeds 1 and 2. Complete matched final-best Child / Parent scores are seed 0: 0.999990 / 0.999999 (-0.000009); seed 1: 0.999994 / 0.996975 (+0.003019); seed 2: 0.993355 / 0.999993 (-0.006639).

All 27 directly recency-only records stay outside subsequent breeding support. per_task.score_gradient_reading:
The visible gradient separates aryl-amine organization from low-scoring fragments and nitrogen tied up in an acyl/sulfonyl environment. Seed 0 evaluation 16 is an N-sulfonyl pyrrolidine ketone at 0.000212; evaluations 12 and 18 are small aryl sulfonyl derivatives near 0.000247. The highest 50 Child products have median 30 heavy atoms and two aromatic rings, and none has N–halogen, O–halogen or O–O bonds. The lowest 50 have median 8.5 heavy atoms. Free aliphatic amine chemistry is available and repeatedly used; it is not a missing generator capability here.

The score tolerates substantial structural complexity, but more modification is not monotonically beneficial. The final seed 0 product at evaluation 300 contains a more rearranged heterocycle/amine assembly and drops to 0.359802. Its score is far below the protected incumbent. Near-unit scores do not establish binding, selectivity, synthesis or chemical stability beyond the supplied objective values.

The Parent leaders retain similar fused-aromatic/cyclic-carbonyl combinations, including ether/N–O bridges and compact fused nitrogen dicarbonyl arrangements. Complete matched final-best Child / Parent scores are seed 0: 0.222020 / 0.225840 (-0.003821); seed 1: 0.225820 / 0.221410 (+0.004410); seed 2: 0.219189 / 0.226003 (-0.006814).

The 25 directly recency-only records never subsequently breed. Seed 0 evaluation 129 is a 56-heavy-atom duplication of aromatic/cyclic-carbonyl modules at 0.143361: it survives in five later live states after local greedy eviction would omit it, but receives no support. The shared changed-rank cohort instead contains 27 evaluated products, with four parent beats and 23 losses. Seed 1 evaluation 234, an N-fluorinated polycycle at 0.217404, beats its best parent at 0.210838, updates the incumbent and later breeds 133 times. Seed 0 evaluation 141, a halogen-free aromatic cyclic dicarbonyl at 0.203056, loses to its parent at 0.205804 yet breeds 50 times. Useful-looking chemistry, local score improvement, and reproductive use are distinct observations. The seed 2 leader at evaluation 292 is terminal and never breeds.
liabilities: Large and fused nitrogen rings, exocyclic unsaturation, N–N connections and the seed 2 four-member nitrogen ring create unresolved conformational and synthetic questions. Ring perception alone does not validate geometry.

There are 571 products with unassigned stereocentres, 37 with N–halogen bonds and 15 tiny fragments. Retaining a doubled aromatic module without any later support does not show productive exploration of its chemistry.
missing_features: The evaluated neighborhood does not show reliable reorganization of the recurring aromatic/cyclic-carbonyl motifs into simpler, stereochemically specified alternatives with comparable observed performance.

Controlled topology variation is limited by repeated module duplication, ring expansion and extra nitrogen links; the present scores do not identify a mandatory missing fragment, and the pool remains unlabeled.
per_task.score_gradient_reading:
The shared initial seed 0 aromatic dione/ester at evaluation 7 scores 0.167839. Later structured aromatic/carbonyl combinations reach about 0.22, whereas ethylene at seed 1 evaluation 267 scores zero. The highest 50 Child products have median 33 heavy atoms, four rings and two aromatic rings; the lowest 50 have median 14 heavy atoms. Four of the highest 50 carry N–halogen bonds; the Parent highest 50 contain none. Initial seed 0 evaluation 7, an aromatic cyclic dione/ester, scores 0.002094. Later fluorinated nitrogen carbonyl/imine organizations rise to the reported leaders. The highest 50 products have median 28 heavy atoms and four rings, versus three heavy atoms in the lowest 50. The one-atom fluorine entry at seed 2 evaluation 253 scores 1.1043196211273875e-26. transferable_gaps.evidence: In n-8fa256ded991, 135 same-contest recency-only records, including 125 generated products, have median three heavy atoms and include 79 tiny structures as well as larger heterocyclic and duplicated modules. Of these, 124 occur in later live populations, but none enters positive support or breeds after protection. Shared survivors with changed ranks instead participate in 126 evaluations with 12 parent beats, four ties and 110 losses. The complete panel preserves both gains and losses. Historical n-03acfe1ba8af had 145 newly kept records without subsequent breeding, and n-28dc36ed5be7 had 602 directly protected records outside support under a different Parent/profile.
transferable_gaps.gap: Preserving a different molecule in the live population does not make its chemistry available to reproduction under the retained rank support.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Any task-agnostic claim that a survival change broadens useful chemistry must follow the preserved molecular records through actual support, parent draws, emitted products and real feedback. Membership, rank movement and descendant ancestry are separate evidence. These counterexamples do not prescribe recency or an age window, and they cannot be promoted into a claim about the whole evolutionary foundation.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Across 4,350 generated evaluated products of n-8fa256ded991, 897 have N–halogen bonds, 456 O–halogen bonds and 319 O–O bonds, versus 1,042, 278 and 273 under n-62daf219c70a. The final populations retain 238, 134 and 63 such records. Halogen-free aromatic/carbonyl leaders and a high-scoring aryl-amine subset without any of these bond flags show that reactive substitutions are not a universal score requirement; a carbon-bound-fluorine leader also remains available.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator can preserve useful aromatic carbonyl and aryl-amine organizations, but does not consistently keep their local bond environments chemically ordinary.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: A transferable chemical capability would preserve the useful connected scaffold and ordinary functional groups while making locally justified bond changes, with observed-score comparisons for those changes. Structural flags can identify environments needing scrutiny, but the mixed leader examples do not support blanket bans, universal plausibility claims or a score benefit inferred from a lower flagged count.

transferable_gaps.evidence: The current evaluated set includes 24 ring-triple-bond-bearing molecules and 25 with a ring carbon carrying two double bonds. Leaders span three-member nitrogen rings, fused four-member rings, nine-member aromatic nitrogen rings and large cyclic carbonyl/amine frameworks. Parent examples also contain questionable constrained unsaturation. Some compact, less unusual structures score well, while higher ring counts and larger duplicated modules can score worse.
transferable_gaps.gap: Valid ring graphs do not provide evidence that the generated ring connections are geometrically or synthetically credible.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Task-agnostic topology changes need a distinction between valid connectivity and chemically credible local geometry, with evidence for retaining useful aromatic/carbonyl/amine relationships through the change. Ring counts and ancestry cannot establish conformational feasibility, a viable synthesis, or conserved-group endpoint mediation.

transferable_gaps.evidence: RDKit detects unassigned centres in 2,553 of the current 4,350 generated evaluated structures, compared with 2,408 for the matched Parent; the supplied Child stereomarker counters are zero. This includes every molecule in one highest-scoring fifty-product subset and 690 final survivor records. The scores do not compare an otherwise matched set of specified stereoisomers.

method_name: Mol GA: rank-selected de novo graph evolution
method_thesis: Anchor the root in Mol GA: maintain a population of oracle-evaluated molecular graphs, sample breeding parents across high-ranked quantiles, generate new offspring through graph crossover and atom/bond mutations, and update survivors greedily after each observation. These are the proposal and selection mechanisms described by [Tripp and Hernández-Lobato (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.09267v1). Start from the supplied initial observations and incorporate newly evaluated offspring immediately, following the evaluator's announced batching. Repeated graph edits and recombination create an evolving search space; no corpus ranking, stored molecule library, pretrained model, or fixed candidate enumeration is needed. The causal hypothesis is that direct selection on task-local scores concentrates successive structural changes around improving molecules quickly enough to raise the final best observed score. The published evidence concerns a larger-budget AUC-Top-10 setting, so its transfer to this benchmark's final Top-1 objective remains a hypothesis.
